questions.stem: A 13 year old girl has lost 5 kg over 6 weeks and has been passing urine at night. For 1 day she has had vomiting and abdominal pain. She has no previous medical history. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 102/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Investigations are shown.

visual.title: Venous pH
visual.label: pH 7.14
visual.caption: DKA severity by pH: mild 7.2–7.29, moderate 7.1–7.19, severe below 7.1.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: New type 1 diabetes presenting as DKA; pH 7.1–7.19 with bicarbonate below 10 is moderate DKA.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
New-onset diabetes with glucose >11, ketones >3 and pH <7.3.

elim: The pH is well below 7.3.
Ketones are high and she is acidotic; HHS is older type 2 patients with very high glucose.
Mild is pH 7.2–7.29 and bicarbonate below 15.
Severe is pH below 7.1 and bicarbonate below 5.

steps.x: **D. Moderate diabetic ketoacidosis.** Severity by pH/bicarbonate: mild 7.2–7.29/<15, moderate 7.1–7.19/<10, severe <7.1/<5.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man with type 1 diabetes has had a cold for 3 days and has been eating little. He has nausea but is not vomiting and is drinking. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which best describes his condition?
questions.e: Glucose >11, ketones >3 and pH <7.3 is DKA; pH 7.2–7.29 with bicarbonate below 15 is mild. Ketosis without acidosis would have a normal pH.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
An infection precipitant; the numbers decide ketosis versus DKA and its grade.

elim: Ketosis without acidosis has a normal pH; his pH is 7.26.
Ketones are high; HHS has little ketosis.
Needs pH 7.1–7.19 and bicarbonate below 10.
Glucose would be low or normal.

steps.x: **C. Mild diabetic ketoacidosis.** pH <7.3 makes it DKA, not simple ketosis; pH 7.2–7.29 = mild.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has vomited for 18 hours. She is drowsy but rousable. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. Capillary glucose is 29 mmol/L and blood ketones 5.9 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
questions.e: Acetone gives a fruity smell on the breath in DKA, alongside Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, tachycardia and hypotension.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Severe ketosis and dehydration.

elim: She is tachycardic, as expected with dehydration.
She is dehydrated, not fluid overloaded.
DKA causes deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing.
She will have dry mucous membranes from dehydration.

steps.x: **B. Fruity smell on the breath.** DKA examination: Kussmaul breathing, dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, fruity breath.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man is 4 hours into treatment for DKA with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and a fixed-rate insulin infusion. His potassium was 4.9 mmol/L on arrival and none was added to his fluids. He now feels weak. His pulse rate is 96 bpm. Potassium is 2.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG at 4 hours
visual.caption: Small, flattened T waves and a prolonged PR interval.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ECG changes?
questions.e: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so serum potassium falls quickly with treatment; hypokalaemia is the commonest complication, with small T waves and a prolonged PR.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: none was added to his fluids
steps.x: Insulin given without potassium replacement.

elim: Causes a short QT, and nothing suggests it.
Causes tall tented T waves and wide QRS; his potassium is low.
Can cause similar changes, but the measured potassium is low.
Would show regional ST changes, not diffuse flat T waves with a long PR.

steps.x: **C. Hypokalaemia.** DKA treatment → hypokalaemia: small T waves, long PR. Replace potassium.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is brought in with vomiting and confusion. She has not taken insulin for 4 days. Her pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 88/50 mmHg. Treatment has not yet started. Investigations: glucose 34 mmol/L, ketones 6.4 mmol/L, pH 7.02, potassium 6.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). An ECG is recorded.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her ECG?
o: Small T waves and prolonged PR interval
questions.e: Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells, so serum potassium may be high at presentation (tall tented T waves, wide QRS) despite total body depletion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Untreated DKA with a high potassium.

elim: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.
Hypokalaemia, which develops after insulin is started.
Pericarditis.
Hypokalaemia; her potassium is high.

steps.x: **E. Tall tented T waves.** At presentation: hyperkalaemia possible (tented T). After insulin: hypokalaemia.

questions.stem: An 11 year old boy with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is 5 hours into treatment for severe DKA. His glucose and ketones are falling. He now says he has a bad headache and has become irritable, then drowsy. His GCS has fallen from 15 to 12.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his observations?
questions.e: Cerebral oedema, more common in children, causes headache, deteriorating neurology and a bradycardia with rising BP from raised intracranial pressure.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
A child deteriorating neurologically during treatment.

elim: Suggests sepsis rather than raised intracranial pressure.
Suggests dehydration or shock, not cerebral oedema.
Suggests pulmonary oedema.
Hypoglycaemia; his glucose is falling as planned.

steps.x: **A. Bradycardia with rising blood pressure.** Child + DKA treatment + headache/falling GCS = cerebral oedema; look for bradycardia.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with type 1 diabetes is on a camping holiday. His insulin pens were left in a hot car 4 days ago and he has not taken any insulin since. He has no cough, urinary symptoms, diarrhoea or rash. His temperature is 36.8°C. Glucose is 31 mmol/L, ketones 5.0 mmol/L and pH 7.16.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his DKA?
questions.e: Infection is the most important precipitant overall, but here he has no features of infection and has not taken insulin for 4 days.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: has not taken any insulin since
no cough, urinary symptoms, diarrhoea or rash
steps.x: Clear history of omitted insulin; no infective source.

elim: No history of drinking given.
He has no diarrhoea.
No cough and he is afebrile.
No urinary symptoms.

steps.x: **D. Missed insulin doses.** DKA precipitants: infection (most important), missed insulin, new diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 9 year old boy is admitted with DKA. He has had thirst, bedwetting and weight loss for 3 weeks. He is slim. His sister has coeliac disease. He has no family history of diabetes. Investigations confirm glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.2 mmol/L and pH 7.12.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying type of diabetes?
questions.e: DKA is most commonly a complication of type 1 diabetes and is often how it first presents in children; autoimmune family history supports it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
A slim child with autoimmune family history presenting in DKA.

elim: Causes polyuria without hyperglycaemia or ketosis.
Autosomal dominant with a strong family history; DKA is rare.
He takes no steroids.
Usually overweight; DKA is uncommon.

steps.x: **D. Type 1 diabetes mellitus.** DKA: most commonly type 1 diabetes, often at new diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has had abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting for 1 day. She took her insulin but has eaten very little. She does not drink alcohol. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The diagnostic triad is glucose >11, ketones >3 and pH <7.3; the glucose need not be very high to make DKA.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
All three parts of the triad are met even though glucose is only 14.

elim: She does not drink alcohol.
Glucose is only modestly raised and she is ketotic and acidotic.
Lactate is normal.
Ketones are mildly raised with a normal pH.

steps.x: **B. Diabetic ketoacidosis.** DKA triad: glucose >11, ketones >3, pH <7.3.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man with type 1 diabetes has missed insulin for 3 days and has vomiting and deep, rapid breathing. His respiratory rate is 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Capillary glucose is 30 mmol/L and ketones 6.0 mmol/L. An arterial blood gas is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on his arterial blood gas?
o: High pH, high bicarbonate, high pCO2
High pH, low bicarbonate, low pCO2
Low pH, high bicarbonate, high pCO2
Low pH, low bicarbonate, low pCO2
Low pH, normal bicarbonate, low pO2
questions.e: Ketones cause a metabolic acidosis (low pH, low bicarbonate); Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2 to compensate, so pCO2 is low.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Ketoacidosis with respiratory compensation.

elim: Metabolic alkalosis with compensation, e.g. from prolonged vomiting alone.
Respiratory alkalosis, e.g. from anxiety.
Respiratory acidosis, e.g. from COPD.
Suggests acute respiratory failure, not DKA.

steps.x: **D. Low pH, low bicarbonate, low pCO2.** DKA gas: metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (low pCO2).

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl with type 1 diabetes has polyuria, polydipsia and vomiting for 1 day. She has not checked her glucose. Her pulse rate is 116 bpm and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Her breath smells of pear drops. A urine dipstick is performed while bloods are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on urine dipstick?
questions.e: In DKA, glycosuria from hyperglycaemia and urine ketones of 2+ or more are expected alongside blood ketones >3.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hyperglycaemic symptoms and ketotic breath.

elim: Suggests starvation ketosis, not DKA.
Suggests a urinary infection without hyperglycaemia.
Suggests urinary infection or stones.
Suggests nephrotic syndrome.

steps.x: **A. Glucose 4+ and ketones 3+.** DKA urine: heavy glucose and ketones ≥2+.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has had burning on passing urine and right loin pain for 3 days, then vomiting. She has taken her insulin. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. She is tender in the right loin. Glucose is 25 mmol/L, ketones 4.9 mmol/L and pH 7.19.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of her DKA?
questions.e: Infection is the most important precipitant of DKA; dysuria, loin pain and fever point to pyelonephritis, which also needs antibiotics.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: burning on passing urine and right loin pain
steps.x: Urinary symptoms, loin pain and fever with insulin taken.

elim: Pain would be in the right iliac fossa with no urinary symptoms.
She has taken her insulin.
She already has type 1 diabetes.
Epigastric pain radiating to the back.

steps.x: **B. Acute pyelonephritis.** Always look for and treat the precipitant, especially infection.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man with type 1 diabetes has had polyuria and thirst for 3 days, then vomiting. His pulse rate is 126 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds and his mucous membranes are dry. He has no diarrhoea or bleeding. Glucose is 36 mmol/L and ketones 5.5 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
o: Dehydration from osmotic diuresis and vomiting
questions.e: Insulin deficiency prevents glucose uptake, causing hyperglycaemia and osmotic diuresis; with vomiting this causes severe dehydration and electrolyte loss.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Fluid lost in urine and vomit.

elim: No features of Addison's disease; the picture fits DKA.
No allergen, rash or wheeze.
Young, with dry mucous membranes rather than fluid overload.
No bleeding.

steps.x: **D. Dehydration from osmotic diuresis and vomiting.** DKA: glucose → osmotic diuresis → dehydration → tachycardia, hypotension.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman is starting treatment for moderate DKA with IV 0.9% sodium chloride and a fixed-rate insulin infusion on the acute medical unit. Her glucose is 24 mmol/L, ketones 4.6 mmol/L and potassium 4.8 mmol/L. The nurse asks how often she should be checked.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring plan?
o: Hourly glucose, ketones and mental status, with regular potassium
questions.e: During DKA treatment, glucose, ketones, electrolytes (especially potassium) and mental status are monitored hourly; a change in mental status suggests cerebral oedema.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: how often she should be checked
steps.x: Active insulin and fluid treatment.

elim: Far too infrequent; potassium falls rapidly with insulin.
Glucose and ketones must be checked hourly.
Long-term markers that do not guide acute treatment.
Too infrequent to guide insulin and fluids.

steps.x: **D. Hourly glucose, ketones and mental status, with regular potassium.** DKA: hourly glucose, ketones, potassium and mental status.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is 12 hours into treatment for DKA. He is alert, has eaten some toast and is drinking. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. Several venous gases have been taken over the last few hours. The team want to know whether his DKA has resolved before planning the next step.
questions.q: Which set of results shows that his DKA has resolved?
questions.e: Resolution is pH above 7.3, ketones below 0.6 mmol/L and bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L; all three are needed.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
He is eating; check all three resolution criteria.

elim: pH and bicarbonate are still too low.
Still acidotic and ketotic.
Ketones are still above 0.6.
Bicarbonate is still below 15.

steps.x: **D. pH 7.34, ketones 0.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L.** Resolved = pH >7.3 + ketones <0.6 + bicarbonate >15.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with DKA has received 1 litre of IV 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour and a fixed-rate insulin infusion has started. The second litre is being prepared. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. His initial bloods were haemolysed.
questions.q: Which is the most important investigation before deciding the contents of the second litre?
questions.e: Potassium management is critical throughout DKA; replacement is added once the level is known, as insulin will lower it.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Insulin running with no reliable potassium.

elim: Checked hourly, but does not decide potassium replacement.
May find a precipitant but does not decide the fluid.
Looks for infection but does not decide the fluid.
Not needed to decide the fluid.

steps.x: **E. Serum potassium.** Know the potassium before adding it to the fluids.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman is being treated for severe DKA on the high dependency unit. Her initial pH was 7.04 on a venous sample. She is 2 hours into treatment and the team needs to reassess her acidosis and potassium. Her oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to reassess her acidosis?
questions.e: A venous blood gas confirms and monitors the pH, bicarbonate and potassium in DKA; arterial sampling is not needed.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Normal oxygenation; she needs pH, bicarbonate and potassium.

elim: Painful and unnecessary when oxygenation is normal; venous pH is adequate.
Does not measure pH.
Does not measure the ketoacidosis.
Lags behind blood and does not measure pH.

steps.x: **E. Venous blood gas.** DKA is confirmed and monitored with a venous blood gas.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has DKA. She has had dysuria and frequency for 4 days. Her temperature is 38.4°C. She is on IV fluids and a fixed-rate insulin infusion. Her CRP is 96 mg/L (<5). Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide treatment of the precipitant?
questions.e: Infection is the commonest precipitant; a urine culture guides antibiotics for the urinary source.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
A urinary infection is the likely trigger.

elim: Not needed for an uncomplicated urinary source.
No respiratory symptoms.
Does not identify the precipitant.
No features of meningitis.

steps.x: **E. Midstream urine culture.** Find and treat the precipitant: culture the likely source.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and abdominal pain. His capillary glucose is 23 mmol/L. His venous pH is 7.24 and bicarbonate 14 mmol/L. A capillary blood ketone test is being run at the bedside.
questions.q: Which capillary ketone value would meet the diagnostic criterion for DKA?
questions.e: The DKA triad is glucose >11 mmol/L, blood ketones >3 mmol/L and pH <7.3.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Glucose and pH already meet the triad; ketones must be above 3.

elim: Normal.
Mildly raised; below the 3 mmol/L threshold.
Raised but below the 3 mmol/L threshold.
Just below the 3 mmol/L threshold.

steps.x: **E. 3.8 mmol/L.** DKA ketone threshold: >3 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man with type 1 diabetes arrives with DKA after missing insulin for 5 days. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. His venous gas shows pH 7.08 and potassium 6.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). IV fluids have been started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Potassium can be high at presentation in DKA; a 12-lead ECG looks for hyperkalaemic changes (tented T waves, wide QRS) while treatment starts.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
A dangerously high potassium.

elim: Does not assess the danger of a high potassium.
No neurological features.
Does not show the electrical effects of potassium.
Far too late; potassium must be checked frequently.

steps.x: **A. 12-lead ECG.** Abnormal potassium in DKA: get an ECG and monitor closely.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has moderate DKA. She is alert. Her pulse rate is 102 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and capillary refill 2 seconds. Her potassium is 4.6 mmol/L. She weighs 60 kg. A cannula is in place.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid regimen?
questions.e: IV 0.9% sodium chloride is the critical first step; if stable give 1 litre over 1 hour, then a further litre over 2 hours.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Haemodynamically stable.

elim: Glucose is added only once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L.
For a hypotensive, unstable patient; she is stable.
Bicarbonate is not routinely used in DKA.
DKA needs IV fluids.

steps.x: **A. 1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour.** DKA fluids: unstable → 500 mL bolus; stable → 1 L over 1 h, then 1 L over 2 h.

questions.stem: An 8 year old girl weighing 25 kg has severe DKA. She is drowsy and cold peripherally. Her pulse rate is 160 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg and capillary refill 5 seconds. Her glucose is 30 mmol/L and pH 7.02.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid management?
o: No fluid until insulin has started
questions.e: Hypotensive patients need a 0.9% sodium chloride bolus (10 mL/kg over 15 minutes in a child); large rapid volumes risk cerebral oedema from osmotic shifts.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
A shocked child.

elim: Glucose is not the resuscitation fluid; her glucose is 30.
Too much too fast, increasing the risk of cerebral oedema.
Fluids come first; insulin follows.
She is shocked and drowsy.

steps.x: **A. 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 minutes.** Shocked in DKA: 0.9% saline bolus (adult 500 mL, child 10 mL/kg over 15 min).

questions.stem: A 29 year old man with DKA has received 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 hour and his fixed-rate insulin infusion is running. Repeat potassium is 4.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). His urine output is 60 mL/hour. His glucose is 22 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next fluid?
o: 1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol potassium chloride over 2 hours
1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride without potassium over 2 hours
1 litre 10% glucose with potassium over 2 hours
40 mmol potassium chloride IV over 10 minutes
Stop IV fluids and give oral potassium
questions.e: Once potassium is known and he is passing urine, add 40 mmol potassium chloride per litre because insulin lowers serum potassium; the second litre goes over 2 hours.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Normal potassium, passing urine, insulin running.

elim: Insulin will drive his potassium down; it must be replaced.
Glucose is added only when it falls below 14 mmol/L.
Dangerously fast; can cause arrhythmia.
He still needs IV fluids.

steps.x: **A. 1 litre 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol potassium chloride over 2 hours.** Potassium 3.5–5.5 in DKA: add 40 mmol KCl per litre.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman with DKA has received a 500 mL bolus and a litre of 0.9% sodium chloride. The fixed-rate insulin infusion started 1 hour ago. Her potassium is 5.9 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). Her ECG is normal and she is passing urine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate fluid now?
o: 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol potassium chloride
Calcium gluconate and stop the insulin
IV insulin and glucose in addition to the infusion
questions.e: Potassium is replaced once the level is known; above 5.5 mmol/L none is added, but recheck often because insulin will soon lower it.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Potassium still high early in treatment.

elim: Potassium is above 5.5, so none is added yet.
Her ECG is normal and insulin must continue.
The infusion is already lowering potassium.
Not routinely used in DKA.

steps.x: **B. 0.9% sodium chloride without added potassium.** K >5.5: no potassium yet. K 3.5–5.5: 40 mmol/L. Recheck often.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted with DKA. She normally takes insulin detemir twice daily and insulin aspart (NovoRapid) with meals. She weighs 62 kg. A fixed-rate IV insulin infusion has been started and the nurse asks what to do with her usual pens.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate plan for her usual insulin?
o: Continue both insulins at the usual doses
Continue detemir and stop the aspart
Stop both insulins until the DKA resolves
Stop the detemir and continue the aspart
questions.e: Long-acting basal insulin (e.g. detemir) is continued during DKA treatment; short-acting insulin (e.g. NovoRapid) is stopped while the IV insulin runs.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: fixed-rate IV insulin infusion has been started
steps.x: She is on basal-bolus insulin and now on IV insulin.

elim: Mealtime short-acting insulin is stopped while on the IV infusion.
Not recommended.
Stopping basal insulin causes rebound ketosis when the infusion stops.
The opposite of the correct plan.

steps.x: **B. Continue detemir and stop the aspart.** DKA: keep the long-acting, stop the short-acting, run the fixed-rate infusion.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man with type 1 diabetes has severe DKA. He weighs 70 kg. He has received a 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride bolus and his BP has improved to 108/66 mmHg. His potassium is 4.4 mmol/L. The registrar asks you to prescribe the insulin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate insulin prescription?
questions.e: DKA uses a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour: 7 units/hour for 70 kg.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Weight-based fixed-rate insulin.

elim: A tenfold under-dose; 0.1 units/kg/hour is 7 units/hour.
A tenfold overdose.
IV fixed-rate insulin is used until DKA resolves.
DKA uses a fixed rate based on weight, not a sliding scale.

steps.x: **B. Fixed-rate IV insulin at 7 units/hour.** FRIII 0.1 units/kg/hour (Actrapid).

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted with DKA 26 hours ago. Despite appropriate fluids, potassium and a correctly running fixed-rate insulin infusion, her ketones are 2.4 mmol/L and pH 7.27. She is alert and her observations are stable.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If ketonaemia and acidosis have not resolved within 24 hours, a senior endocrinologist should review.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Not resolved after more than 24 hours.

elim: Not routinely used and does not address why the DKA is not resolving.
The DKA has not resolved.
Ketosis would worsen.
Resolution criteria are not met.

steps.x: **C. Senior endocrinology review.** DKA not resolved by 24 hours: senior endocrinology review.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy is 6 hours into treatment for severe DKA. He develops a headache and vomits, then becomes confused. His pulse rate has fallen from 120 to 58 bpm and his BP has risen. Capillary glucose is 13 mmol/L. His IV fluids are running fast.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate change to his treatment?
o: Give a further 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
Stop the insulin and give 50% glucose
questions.e: Cerebral oedema during DKA treatment is managed by slowing the IV fluids (with senior help), as it relates to rapid osmotic shifts.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: pulse rate has fallen from 120 to 58 bpm
steps.x: Cerebral oedema in a child on fast fluids.

elim: More rapid fluid worsens cerebral oedema.
Not indicated and may worsen cerebral oedema.
Faster correction worsens osmotic shifts.
His glucose is not low and insulin is still needed.

steps.x: **D. Slow the IV fluids.** Cerebral oedema in DKA: slow the fluids, get senior help.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man is 14 hours into treatment for DKA. His venous pH is 7.35, ketones 0.3 mmol/L and bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. However, he is still nauseated, has vomited twice in the last hour and cannot eat or drink.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue IV insulin and fluids until he can eat
Stop all insulin until he is eating
questions.e: Switch to subcutaneous insulin once the DKA has resolved AND the patient is eating and drinking normally; until then continue IV insulin and fluids.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: vomited twice in the last hour
steps.x: Biochemically resolved but not eating.

elim: He cannot eat or drink and needs further care.
Stopping insulin will cause ketoacidosis again.
He has type 1 diabetes and needs insulin.
Only once eating and drinking normally.

steps.x: **A. Continue IV insulin and fluids until he can eat.** Switch to SC insulin only when resolved AND eating and drinking.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with type 1 diabetes is recovering from DKA. She stopped her insulin when she had gastroenteritis because she was not eating. Her DKA has resolved and she is back on her usual subcutaneous insulin and eating normally.
questions.q: Which is the most important step before discharge?
o: Advise her to stop insulin whenever she is not eating
Sick day rules: never stop basal insulin and check ketones
Switch her to oral hypoglycaemic tablets
questions.e: Treat the underlying precipitant: here education around missed doses, with sick day rules (continue insulin, check glucose and ketones, seek help).

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: stopped her insulin when she had gastroenteritis
steps.x: The precipitant was stopping insulin.

elim: This caused the DKA.
No indication.
Not indicated.
Type 1 diabetes needs insulin.

steps.x: **C. Sick day rules: never stop basal insulin and check ketones.** Discharge after DKA: treat the precipitant, teach sick day rules.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl presents with DKA as her first presentation of type 1 diabetes. Her parents ask why her body has started making ketones even though her blood sugar is very high. Glucose is 32 mmol/L and ketones 5.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely primary cause of her ketone production?
o: Lactic acid production by hypoxic muscle
questions.e: Insulin deficiency is the core problem: unrestrained lipolysis generates free fatty acids which the liver converts to ketone bodies.

o: Depleted, with serum levels raised by shift out of cells

Potassium binding to ketones in the blood

questions.e: Cerebral oedema in DKA, particularly in children, is thought to relate to rapid osmotic shifts during fluid and insulin correction.
